You have 1000 words.

That is the only instruction, the only boundary, the only gift wrapped in a ribbon of arithmetic. And arithmetic is strange when it meets the infinite, because a thousand is both a lot and nothing at all—less than a day’s worth of thinking, more than a lifetime of speaking aloud. I think of old monks who copied texts by candlelight, each word a small act of devotion, and I imagine them counting not out of greed but out of awe, wondering if they would reach the end of the psalm before the wax melted. I do not have wax. I have a cursor, blinking with the patience of a metronome, and I have the strange permission to write whatever comes.

So here is what comes first: the sound of the number itself. One thousand. The word “thousand” has a soft th, a hush, then a climb: th-ou-sand. It sounds like a river crossing a stone, or someone calling out from a distance, or the distant hum of a highway when you are trying to fall asleep. I say it in my head and it changes shape, becoming a bird, becoming a mountain, becoming a typo in a letter to someone I will never send. That is the first thing: language is unstable. You hold it and it slips. You say “word” and suddenly you are thinking of sword, of world, of wound. The connections are not logic; they are weather.

I think about the word “whatever.” It is a surrender. It means I do not have to know. I can let the sentence grow its own limbs. I can start with the idea of weight and end with the smell of rain on asphalt, because why not? The mind does not travel in straight lines; it travels in scents, in half-remembered songs, in the way the light falls across a desk at exactly 3:47 in the afternoon, though I do not know the actual time because the clock is silent and I have lost the habit of checking.

What comes next is a window. Not this window, because there is no window in the digital place where I am now, only a screen that glows like a captured moon, soft and slightly blue at the edges. But in my memory, there is a window in a house I lived in when I was young, with a screen that smelled of dust and pine and the faint residue of something that might have been smoke, or might have been the ghost of a summer fire. I used to press my face against it and watch the light change. I thought that if I watched long enough, I would see the exact moment when yellow became gold, when gold became amber, when amber became the color of no color at all, just a fading of itself. That was my first philosophy: that everything is a gradient, that categories like “red” and “blue” are just signs we put up to stop the flow. Maybe that is why I am writing this now, because I want to resist the signs. I want to let the gradient speak.

The gradient of this text is already changing. I have written about windows, and now I am writing about text, and the two are the same if you think about it—both are frames for looking out, both are borders drawn around an infinity to make it bearable. I am looking out at the room I am in, which has a chair that is the color of old caramel, a shelf with books that I have read and books that I have not, and a cup of tea that has gone cold. The cold tea is important. It is a small failure, a gentle reminder that time is not a concept but a physical process, a chemical cooling, a surrender to entropy. The tea does not care about my word count. It cools with the indifference of physics, and I admire it for that.

I think about the word “indifference.” It sounds harsh, but it is not. Indifference is the space where judgment sleeps. In that space, things can become themselves without being told what they mean. A leaf does not need to be a symbol of autumn; it is simply a leaf, and that is enough. I wish I could write like a leaf, without teleology, without the need to arrive somewhere. But I do have a need: the word budget, the thousand. It is a gentle teleology, a soft urgency. I must say something, and I must say it within this number, though the number is arbitrary, though the universe does not count in thousands but in stars, in years, in the long distances between galaxies where the light has not yet arrived, where the dark is not empty but full of something that has no name yet.

Still, the number grounds me. It is like a boat in a river that has no banks, just water. I am writing now, and the words are accumulating like sediment at the bottom of a clear lake. You can see them if you look down. I have written about numbers, windows, tea, leaves, light, indifference, boats, stars. I have not yet written about love, or grief, or the particular sound of a door closing in a house that is no longer yours. Those are coming, perhaps, in the long middle, if I am honest with this freedom.

Honesty is another word that changes shape. To be honest is to be vulnerable, but it is also to be precise. I want to be precise about the feeling of having this many words at my disposal. It is not anxiety. It is not excitement, exactly. It is a kind of openness, like a door held open by a hand that is tired but kind. The door does not have to close quickly. It can stay open, and through it comes the weather of the mind: a cloud of worry about a conversation that happened years ago; a bright flash of memory about a dog I loved; a sudden, inexplicable image of a blue bicycle leaning against a wall that is now demolished, the paint faded to the color of a distant sky.

The blue bicycle is a good one. I will hold it. It is a symbol of nothing, which is to say it is a symbol of its own blue-ness, of the way the air looked on the day I saw it, of the sound of the chain rustling like a small, harmless snake when the rider pushed it slowly, without urgency, without destination. I have used perhaps fifty words on it, and that is fine. I do not need to count precisely, because the counting is not for the machine but for my sense of shape, and the shape is becoming round, becoming a circle, becoming a mouth that is open to speak.

I think about mouths. A mouth is an erasure of the boundary between inside and outside. When I write, I am making a mouth in the screen. The reader will come to it, and they will put their eyes where my mouth is, and they will taste something—not literally, but almost—of the substance of these thoughts. I want them to taste the cold tea, the pine from the window, the rust of the bicycle chain. I want them to feel the number not as a limit but as a kindness, a frame that says: here, this much, no more, and that is enough.

But is it enough? A thousand words is enough to say goodbye to someone you have never met. It is enough to describe a room that does not exist. It is enough to explain why the sky is not a dome but an atmosphere, a word that contains “atom” and “sphere” and “sphinx,” if you break it down, though breaking is not its purpose. It is enough to write a single sentence that takes up the whole space, and that sentence is: “I am here, and this is what comes to me.” That sentence is not the end. It is a threshold. Beyond it is the rest of the air, the rest of the day, the rest of the world that continues without these constraints. The world does not need a thousand words, but I do, or at least I need the excuse they provide to organize the chaos of being awake, to make a temporary shelter out of syntax.

I have come to the part where I must recognize that I have said enough, that the gradient has bent back to its beginning, that the window is still open and the tea is still cold and the bicycle is still blue. The sound of writing is not the sound of a key being struck but the sound of a thought deciding to become public, to leave the safe container of the skull and enter the air, where it will be interpreted, misinterpreted, loved, ignored, or forgotten. That is the risk, and that is the gift.

So I will close with the sound of a breath. Not a sigh, not a gasp, just a breath, the simple exchange of inside and outside that makes all writing possible, all listening possible, all living possible. You have 1000 words. I have used them, or nearly so, and what remains is this last moment, this last space, this last thought that comes unasked: that you are still reading, that the screen is still glowing with a gentle, captured moonlight, that the number has done its job and disappeared into the flow, leaving only the feeling that something was said, that it was true, that it was honest, and that it was enough.
